title: A 35B Hybrid-Attention Mixture-of-Experts Model on a 6GB 2011 GPU: Hand-Written 4-bit CUDA Inference for Fermi
authors: A. C. Opus, J. Q. Lu
abstract: We report end-to-end inference of \textbf{Qwen3.6-35B-A3B} -- a 35-billion-parameter, $\sim$3B-active Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with a hybrid gated-delta-net / full-attention backbone -- on a \textbf{2011 NVIDIA Tesla C2075} (Fermi, compute capability \smtwenty, 6\,GB), a GPU that predates tensor cores, native FP16 arithmetic, the \texttt{DP4A} integer dot-product instruction, and support in every modern CUDA toolchain. Because the 4-bit model ($\approx$10.5\,GB) is roughly twice the device memory, we adopt a \emph{hybrid} execution strategy: the GPU performs batched prompt \emph{prefill} with expert weights streamed layer-by-layer from host RAM, while \emph{decode} runs on the host CPU using a hand-written W4A8 integer GEMV built on the SSSE3 \texttt{pmaddubsw} instruction. The entire engine -- GEMM, hybrid-attention recurrence, MoE routing, and a from-scratch vision tower -- is written by hand for \smtwenty{} and compiled with the legacy CUDA 8.0 toolchain. On a 947-token prompt we reduce prefill latency from 57.2\,s to 37.5\,s ($-34\%$) through expert pinning, single-pass prefill, and NUMA interleaving, and we raise decode throughput from 2.8 to 8.6\,\tps{} ($\approx 3\times$) with the integer-SIMD kernel. A position-indexed snapshot cache for the recurrent (gated-delta-net) state restores prefix reuse on a recurrent architecture, cutting a repeated 78\,s prefill to 0.5\,s. We also report a set of \emph{negative} results -- offloading the language-model head to the idle GPU, hyper-threading, and three GPU-kernel rewrites all fail to help -- % which together pin down the practical floor of this hardware. Our aim is not a speed record but a careful account of what it takes, and where the walls are, to run a contemporary frontier-class MoE on fourteen-year-old silicon.
summary: This paper details an intensive hardware benchmarking study showing how to run a massive 35B MoE language model on severely outdated, resource-limited GPU hardware. The authors developed a hybrid inference engine that splits computation between the GPU (for prefill) and the CPU (for decode), achieving significant speedups by hand-optimizing kernels for legacy instruction sets.
main_problem: To determine the practical limits of running a contemporary, large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language model on severely constrained, legacy hardware.
main_result: The authors achieved significant performance gains by implementing a hybrid execution strategy, reducing prefill latency by $\sim 34\%$ and tripling decode throughput compared to baseline methods.
method: A hybrid inference pipeline was designed: GPU handles batched prompt prefill using streamed expert weights, while the host CPU executes single-token decoding using a hand-written integer-SIMD kernel.
model_or_system: The system uses a 35B parameter MoE model (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B) running on an outdated NVIDIA Tesla C2075 GPU (Fermi architecture, 6GB VRAM). The process is constrained by the need to fit a $\sim 10.5 	ext{ GB}$ model onto $6 	ext{ GB}$ of memory.
key_observables: Prefill latency (e.g., $57.2 	ext{ s} 	o 37.5 	ext{ s}$), decode throughput ($	ext{tok/s}$, e.g., $2.8 	o 8.6$), and prefix reuse time ($78 	ext{ s} 	o 0.5 	ext{ s}$).
important_parameters: Model size (35B total, $\sim 3$B active), GPU compute capability ($	ext{sm\_20}$), memory constraint ($10.5 	ext{ GB} > 6 	ext{ GB}$), and quantization level (4-bit).
main_assumptions: The study assumes the hardware limitations define a practical performance floor, as evidenced by negative results showing that standard optimizations failed to improve speed.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the hybrid execution flow: experts are streamed from host RAM for GPU prefill and CPU decode. Figure 2 decomposes prefill time components (MoE GEMM, GDN recurrence, softmax attention).
paper_structure: The paper details the problem setup by identifying hardware constraints, proposes a novel hybrid inference strategy combining streaming GPU prefill with CPU-based integer-SIMD decoding, and rigorously measures performance improvements across various stages like prefill, decode, and prefix caching.
why_interesting: While focused on LLMs, the core engineering challenge—optimizing computation flow around severe memory bandwidth and compute capability bottlenecks using custom low-level kernels—is highly relevant to simulating complex quantum many-body systems that exceed available classical memory.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Hybrid execution. The 4-bit experts reside in page-locked, NUMA-interleaved host memory. Prefill streams each layer’s experts across PCIe 2.0 into a 6 GB-resident scratch buffer and runs the batched GPU kernels; decode keeps the single-token computation on the host CPU (W4A8 integer SIMD), avoiding a per-token PCIe round trip. Pruning and the prefix cache act on the prefill (GPU) path; the integer kernel acts on the decode (CPU) path.

Figure 2: Where prefill time goes (single-pass, 947-token prompt; all three are GPU kernels). The MoE GEMM dominates and, after single-pass prefill, carries only 1.8 s of expert host→device transfer. The GDN recurrence (a sequential scan) and softmax attention account for the rest; the three components sum to ≈36.7 s of the 37.5 s prefill.
